A /24 is the subnet almost everyone meets first: 256 addresses, 254 of them usable for hosts, with the familiar mask 255.255.255.0. It maps neatly onto the last octet, which is why home routers, small offices and most lab topologies use it.

A /27 gives you 32 addresses and 30 usable hosts. It is the sweet spot for a small team's VLAN, a guest Wi-Fi segment or a rack of management interfaces, and it appears constantly in certification exams because its boundaries are easy to get wrong.

A /27 has 32 addresses (2 to the power of 5) and 30 usable hosts, because one address is the network address and one is the broadcast address. Its subnet mask is 255.255.255.224 and its wildcard mask is 0.0.0.31. A /24 can be divided into eight /27 subnets.

A subnet mask uses 1s for network bits and 0s for host bits. A wildcard mask is the exact inverse: 0 means "this bit must match", 1 means "ignore this bit". For /24 the mask is 255.255.255.0 and the wildcard is 0.0.0.255; for /27 they are 255.255.255.224 and 0.0.0.31. Cisco IOS uses wildcard masks in access lists and in OSPF/EIGRP network statements, for example access-list 10 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 or network 10.1.0.0 0.0.255.255 area 0. The quick conversion is to subtract each octet of the subnet mask from 255 – the IPv4 tab shows both side by side and accepts either form as input.

Firewalls, cloud security groups and route tables want CIDR notation, but vendors, ISPs and spreadsheets often give you a range like 192.168.1.100 to 192.168.1.199. Unless the range happens to be a power-of-two block starting on an aligned boundary, it takes several CIDRs to express precisely.

For a requirement of n hosts, find the smallest power of two that is at least n + 2 (network and broadcast), then the prefix is 32 minus that exponent. For 28 hosts: 28 + 2 = 30, the next power of two is 32 = 2^5, so the prefix is 32 − 5 = /27.

For each requirement, pick the smallest block that holds hosts + 2 (network and broadcast). 50 hosts → 64 addresses → /26; 25 → 32 → /27; 10 → 16 → /28; 2 → 4 → /30 (or /31 on point-to-point links, RFC 3021).

IPv6 addresses are 128 bits written as eight hexadecimal groups, with leading zeros dropped and one run of zero groups collapsible to :: (RFC 5952 compression). The first 64 bits identify the network and the last 64 the interface. Unlike IPv4 there is no broadcast address: IPv6 uses multicast (for example ff02::1 for all nodes on the link) and there are no reserved network/broadcast addresses, so every address in a prefix is usable. LANs use a /64 so that SLAAC (stateless autoconfiguration) can build the interface identifier; organizations typically receive a /48 (65,536 /64 subnets) or a /56. Point-to-point links are often numbered from a /127. Write the IP address and the subnet mask in binary. The network address is the bitwise AND of the two; the broadcast address is the network address with all host bits set to 1. For 192.168.1.10/26 the mask is 255.255.255.192, the network is 192.168.1.0, the broadcast is 192.168.1.63 and the usable hosts run from .1 to .62. The number of addresses in a block is 2 to the power of (32 minus the prefix length), and usable hosts are that number minus 2.
